stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Hester Vane's 1921 novel The Linen Year. Ada, a young apprentice at a textile mill, has inherited her grandmother's hand loom.

For months Ada had thought the old loom a relic, fit only for the attic; the mill wove a hundred yards before her grandmother's shuttle crossed a single width. Yet one evening, smoothing a coverlet her grandmother had made, she found a tiny knot repeated at every border, placed where no mill would allow a flaw. It was, she understood, a signature. That night she sat down at the loom and did not rise until the candle guttered.
choices: To convey a grandmother's pride in the distinctive marks she wove into her cloth
To portray a character whose dismissive view of an inherited loom gives way to regard for it
To contrast the speed of mill production with the slowness of weaving by hand
To depict a character's growing frustration with the demands of her work at the mill
explanation: The setup puts Ada at the center. The excerpt opens with what she has long believed (the loom is a relic), turns on "Yet," and ends with her working at the loom all night. The excerpt as a whole shows her contempt for the loom turning into respect, which is what B says.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ada to her grandmother. The knot is something Ada discovers, and the text never describes what the grandmother felt. The excerpt is about Ada's change of heart.

C.why: You picked a detail from the first sentence. The speed comparison only explains why Ada looked down on the loom. It isn't what the excerpt is for.

D.why: You read in a feeling the text never states. Nothing suggests Ada resents the mill. The mill only comes up as the point of comparison behind her early view of the loom.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Clear thematic reversal triggered by grandmother's signature; one step with subtlety of what makes the loom precious.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Rydell's 1958 poem "To a Fern in Shale." The speaker addresses a fossilized fern.

You have been told, small frond, that you are gone, / pressed flat, a rumor in the stone. / But I have seen your cousins in the ravine / unrolling every April, green / as if no age had passed. So do not grieve / the weight above you: what you were still lives.
choices: To lament that the fern's kind vanished long ago beneath layers of stone
To celebrate the speaker's discovery of living ferns growing in a ravine
To explain how ferns came to be preserved in shale over long periods
To reassure the fern that its kind has endured despite its own apparent loss
explanation: The poem opens with what the fern "has been told": that it is gone. After "But," the speaker offers evidence against that view (living ferns every April), and the poem ends by telling the fern "do not grieve" because "what you were still lives." The tone is consoling, and the fern is the one being consoled.

A.why: You flipped the tone. The first two lines state a belief that sounds like a lament, but the rest of the poem argues against it and tells the fern not to grieve.

B.why: You shifted the focus from the addressee to the speaker. The ravine ferns are evidence offered to comfort the fossil. They are not the poem's subject.

C.why: You credited the poem with an explanation it never gives. "Pressed flat" and "stone" name the fern's condition but don't describe how fossilization happens.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Purpose of reassurance is signaled by 'do not grieve,' though tone requires noticing speaker addresses the fossil itself.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Inês Carvalho's 1987 memoir. Carvalho's father was a surveyor who drew maps for the provincial government.

My father's maps were famous in the ministry for their precision; not a stream was misplaced. As a child, I assumed he loved the land the way he loved his instruments, coolly and exactly. However, clearing his desk after he died, I found a second set of sheets, never submitted. On them he had marked where the Almeida girl drowned, where my mother first agreed to walk with him, where the best figs grew.
choices: To convey the narrator's discovery that the father's bond with the land was deeply personal
To portray the father's pride in the precision that earned praise from the ministry
To suggest that the father hid the private maps for fear of the ministry's disapproval
To show that the narrator's childhood view of the father was confirmed by the desk's contents
explanation: The narrator describes a long-held belief (the father loved the land "coolly and exactly"), then "However" brings in the private maps full of memories and personal landmarks. The excerpt as a whole shows the narrator learning that the father's attachment to the land went well beyond the official measurements.

B.why: You focused on the father's reputation, which appears only in the opening. The text never says the father felt proud, and the passage moves past that precision to what the narrator finds.

C.why: You supplied a motive the text never gives. The sheets were "never submitted," but nothing says why.

D.why: You got the direction of the turn backward. "However" marks the discovery as a correction of the childhood belief, not a confirmation of it.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Multi-step: must recognize two maps represent different kinds of knowledge, infer what discovery reveals about assumption.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Lionel Achterberg's 1974 short story "The Trench." Maren, a graduate student, is excavating a Bronze Age site with her professor, Dr. Hale.

Dr. Hale had spent thirty seasons at the site. When Maren's trowel struck the rim of a clay bowl, he knelt beside her and said nothing for a long while. Maren waited for praise. Instead he asked her to describe what she saw, then to describe it again, more slowly. By the third telling she noticed a thumbprint pressed into the rim, and she understood that he had not been testing her; he had been giving her the find.
choices: To convey Dr. Hale's long devotion to a site where he has worked for decades
To depict Maren's disappointment that her discovery went without any praise
To portray Maren's realization that her mentor's silence let her claim the find
To explain how archaeologists work out who made an ancient clay object
explanation: The setup and the final sentence both center on Maren. She expects praise, gets questions instead, and at last understands that Hale "had been giving her the find." The excerpt builds toward her new understanding of his silence.

A.why: You shifted the focus to the professor. His thirty seasons are background. The excerpt's point is what Maren comes to understand about him.

B.why: You stopped reading halfway through. Maren does wait for praise, but the ending replaces that expectation with understanding, so disappointment isn't what the excerpt conveys.

D.why: You treated a story as a method guide. The thumbprint is a detail Maren notices, and the text never explains any technique for identifying a maker.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Multi-step realization that mentor's silence intentionally lets student claim the discovery

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Clara Ondaatje's 1996 poem "Burn Season." The speaker addresses a child walking with her through a recently burned forest.

Do not look away from the blackened hill, / the pines like struck matches, the hush where the jays were. / Look closer: beneath the ash the fireweed / has already pushed its red thumbs up. / The lodgepole cones, sealed shut for years, / opened only in this heat. / What frightens you is how a forest begins.
choices: To warn the child about the destruction that fire can bring to a forest
To encourage the child to see the burned hill as a place of renewal
To mourn the loss of the birds that once filled the forest on the hill
To explain why lodgepole pines must have fire in order to reproduce
explanation: The poem opens on destruction, then turns at "Look closer" to new growth, and closes by recasting the frightening scene as "how a forest begins." The speaker's commands ("Do not look away," "Look closer") are encouraging, not cautionary, and they ask the child to see the burn as a beginning.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The opening images are grim, but the speaker uses them to lead the child from fear toward seeing renewal, not to warn.

C.why: You took one image as the whole poem. The missing jays are part of the opening description of damage, and the poem moves on to new growth.

D.why: You claimed more than the poem says. It notes that the cones opened in the heat but never says the pines need fire, and its purpose isn't to explain biology.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Parsing encouragement toward renewal beneath dark imagery and interpretive traps

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Anneliese Brandt's 1909 novel The Copyist. Teodor copies out orchestral parts from the manuscripts of the composer Voss.

Teodor had copied Voss's scores for eleven years and believed his task purely mechanical: a note in, a note out. But in the slow movement of the new symphony he found a passage that could not be right, the oboe climbing where every rule said it must fall. To correct it would take a single stroke. He copied it as written, and all night the note sang in his head, until he could not tell whether it was Voss's mistake or his genius.
choices: To portray a copyist left torn over whether a passage he reproduced is a flaw or brilliance
To convey a composer's confidence in breaking the accepted rules of composition
To show a copyist correcting a composer's error despite doubts about his own judgment
To depict a copyist's resentment of years of careful work that went unrecognized
explanation: Teodor, the focus of the setup, starts out believing his work is mechanical. After "But," an odd passage unsettles him, and the excerpt ends with him unable to decide between "mistake" and "genius." What it shows is his being torn.

B.why: You moved the focus from Teodor to Voss. The text never shows Voss's attitude. It shows only Teodor's uncertainty about what Voss meant.

C.why: You missed the key action. Teodor "copied it as written." He considers correcting the note but doesn't do it.

D.why: You added an emotion the text doesn't give. The eleven years set up his belief that the work is mechanical, and nothing suggests he resents it.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Multi-step uncertainty about whether rule-breaking passage represents error or undiscovered genius

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Dorothy Quill's 1968 memoir of years spent in an industrial metals laboratory.

In the laboratory we were taught to trust the numbers: tensile strength, hardness, the exact temperature at which a steel turns brittle. I trusted them. Yet the old blacksmith who came each spring to sharpen our shop tools could judge a blade's temper by its color alone: straw, then bronze, then a blue like evening. He had never read a chart. I kept my instruments, but I began, quietly, to watch the colors too.
choices: To portray a blacksmith's disdain for the instruments used in the laboratory
To suggest the narrator gave up measurement in favor of traditional methods
To describe the sequence of colors that steel passes through when tempered
To convey the narrator's growing respect for a practical skill the lab never taught
explanation: The narrator starts with the laboratory's lesson (trust the numbers), then "Yet" introduces the blacksmith's skill, and the excerpt ends with the narrator starting to "watch the colors too." It shows the narrator coming to value a different kind of knowledge while still keeping the instruments.

A.why: You shifted the focus to the blacksmith and gave him an attitude the text never shows. He "had never read a chart," but nothing says he looks down on the instruments.

B.why: You overlooked "I kept my instruments." The narrator adds the blacksmith's method to measurement rather than replacing measurement with it.

C.why: You fell for the content trap. The colors are accurately listed, but they're a detail showing the blacksmith's skill, not the reason the excerpt exists.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Subtle understanding that respecting practical skill doesn't require abandoning instruments

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Samuel Okafor's 2004 novel Grid. Nkem, a city planner, has returned to the neighborhood where she grew up, which her office has proposed to redevelop.

On paper the district was a problem to be solved: narrow lots, no setbacks, streets that defied every standard in the manual. Nkem had drawn the new plan herself. Now, standing at the corner where Mrs. Adeyemi still sold roasted corn from a cart, she watched children cut through the crooked alleys the plan would straighten. Every flaw on her map, she saw, was someone's shortcut home. She folded the drawing and put it away.
choices: To convey Mrs. Adeyemi's attachment to the corner where she has long sold food
To show that Nkem has decided to cancel the redevelopment she proposed
To portray Nkem's growing doubt about her plan as she sees how residents use the area
To explain why the district failed to meet the standards in the planning manual
explanation: The excerpt opens with the official view (the district is "a problem to be solved"), then shows Nkem watching residents use the streets her plan would change. Her realization that "every flaw on her map" is "someone's shortcut home," followed by her folding up the drawing, shows her starting to doubt her own design.

A.why: You shifted the focus to a minor character. Mrs. Adeyemi's cart marks where Nkem stands, and the text never describes Mrs. Adeyemi's feelings.

B.why: You read too much into the ending. Folding the drawing signals doubt, but the text never says Nkem cancels the project.

D.why: You chose the opening detail. The list of shortfalls sets up the official view that Nkem's experience then challenges. Explaining those shortfalls isn't the excerpt's purpose.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Multi-step recognition that map 'flaws' serve residents, prompting plan reconsideration

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Marguerite Ostell's 1931 novel *The Lantern Year*. Wren, a young assistant at a hilltop observatory, is waiting for a comet that the observatory's director has predicted will appear.

For three nights the eyepiece had shown Wren nothing but the old familiar stars, and the director's notebook, with its neat columns of predicted positions, had begun to look to her like a kind of boast. On the fourth night she nearly did not climb the stairs. Yet when the faint smudge finally swam into the field, exactly where the columns said it would be, she did not call down to anyone. She stayed bent at the eyepiece a long while, ashamed of her doubt and quietly amazed.
choices: To portray the director's satisfaction at seeing his prediction of the comet's position proved correct
To convey Wren's growing impatience with the routine and uneventful work of nightly observation
To depict Wren's shift from doubting the director's prediction to a private, humbled wonder at its accuracy
To show Wren deciding to keep the comet's appearance hidden from the director and the other staff
explanation: The setup makes Wren the focus. Read as a whole, the excerpt follows her change: at first she sees the director's predictions as "a kind of boast" and almost skips the night, and then the comet appears exactly where predicted and she stays at the eyepiece "ashamed of her doubt and quietly amazed." Choice C names the right person and the full movement from doubt to humbled wonder.

A.why: You moved the focus to the wrong person. The director's prediction proves correct, but he never appears in the scene, and the text says nothing about how he feels. Everything is shown through Wren.

B.why: You stopped after the opening. Wren's impatience is only the starting point. The excerpt is built around what happens when the comet appears, and this choice leaves that turn out.

D.why: You read too much into "she did not call down to anyone." She waits before sharing the moment. Nothing suggests she decides to hide the comet, and the closing feelings are shame and amazement, not secrecy.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Tomas Velde's 1968 poem "To a Girl Drawing Streets." The speaker addresses a young city planner.

You set your ruler on the paper town
and trust the avenues to keep their line.
They won't. Walkers will wear their own paths down
through lawns and corners of your neat design.
Don't grieve for that. Leave something unassigned—
a square, a strip of ground with no set use—
and let the city finish what you've designed:
the shortcut, and the bench the old men choose.
choices: To warn the young planner that residents will eventually undo even her most careful designs
To encourage the young planner to leave room for residents to shape the city in their own ways
To criticize city officials who ignore the needs of residents when they approve new plans
To describe the shortcuts and benches that the speaker admires most in an older city
explanation: The poem speaks to the young planner. The first half predicts that walkers will wear their own paths through her design. Then "Don't grieve for that" turns the poem: the speaker tells her to leave ground "unassigned" and "let the city finish" her work. The tone is encouraging, and Choice B captures both the addressee and that advice.

A.why: You reversed the tone. The first four lines do sound like a warning, but "Don't grieve for that" turns the poem into advice to welcome the change, not to fear it. The poem as a whole encourages her.

C.why: You brought in people the poem never mentions. No officials or approvals appear, and the speaker gives gentle advice to one planner rather than criticizing anyone.

D.why: You took a closing detail for the whole poem. The shortcut and the bench are examples of what residents add. The poem is about advice to the planner, not about the speaker's favorite features of some older city.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Harlan Prieto's 1987 memoir. Prieto recalls watching a test of a bridge his father designed.

The morning of the load test, trucks heavy with gravel rolled onto the new span one after another, and I gripped the riverbank railing as if I could hold the bridge up myself. My father stood beside me with his hands in his pockets. I took his stillness for bravery and admired him for it. Only years later, studying for my own engineering exams, did I understand that he had not been brave at all. He had checked the arithmetic, every line of it, until nothing was left to fear.
choices: To portray the father's quiet pride as a bridge he had designed passed a public test
To show the narrator's fear that the bridge would give way under the loaded trucks
To explain why the narrator chose to follow his father into the engineering profession
To convey how the narrator later came to see his father's calm as preparation, not courage
explanation: The narrator is the focus, and the excerpt is built on a change in how he understands what he saw. As a boy he "took his stillness for bravery." Years later he realizes his father "had not been brave at all" because he had checked every calculation. Choice D names the narrator and that reinterpretation.

A.why: You moved the focus to the father and gave him a feeling the text never mentions. We see only his stillness, and the passage is about how the narrator interprets that stillness, not about any pride the father feels.

B.why: You stopped at the first sentence. The boy's fear sets up the contrast with his father, but the excerpt's point is what he understood years later. This choice leaves out the turn the passage is built around.

C.why: You treated a passing detail as the purpose. The text mentions that he later studied engineering, but it never says why he chose it. That detail is only when his realization came.

subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ada Lindqvist's 1954 short story "Test Plots." Nell, home from agricultural college, has persuaded her uncle to let her try a new planting method on part of his field.

Every evening Nell walked the line between the two halves of the field: her uncle's wheat on one side, and on the other, wheat she had sown where clover grew the year before. By July the difference could not be missed. Her side stood taller and darker, and she knew the figures in her notebook would please her professors. But her uncle had farmed that ground for forty years, and she found herself hoping, a little, that he would not walk out far enough to see.
choices: To portray Nell as torn between satisfaction in her results and reluctance to see her uncle shown up
To convey the uncle's resentment of the farming methods that his niece learned at college
To show that Nell's method produced a better wheat crop than her uncle's usual approach
To describe the particular techniques that Nell learned from her professors at college
explanation: The setup makes Nell the focus. The excerpt pulls her two ways: her side of the field is clearly better and will "please her professors," but because her uncle has farmed the land for forty years, she hopes "he would not walk out far enough to see." Choice A names Nell and both sides of that mixed feeling.

B.why: You moved the focus to the uncle and gave him a feeling the text never shows. He never appears or reacts. The worry about his response is Nell's, not his resentment.

C.why: You chose a true statement about the content that misses the purpose. The better crop is the situation, but the excerpt ends on Nell's reluctance to have her uncle see it. Someone who skipped the last sentence would choose this.

D.why: You assumed details the text never gives. Apart from sowing wheat where clover grew, no techniques are described, and the professors appear only as people the results would please.
